analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to own a handgun or detachable-magazine semiautomatic rifle and records every sale.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal crime to own a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that takes a detachable magazine without a firearm owner license, issued after a fingerprint background check. It would also require every sale or transfer of those guns to go through a licensed dealer, who would report it to a new federal record-of-sale system. It added offenses for failing to report a lost or stolen gun and for leaving a loaded gun where a child can reach it, with prison terms of up to 10 years for licensing violations.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities affected by gun violence, since licensing and recorded-sale systems are designed to keep guns from prohibited buyers and make crime guns traceable; also police, who get a paper trail for tracing. The bill's findings point to disproportionate gun deaths among Black and Latino children and teens. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Requires every owner of a handgun or detachable-magazine semiautomatic rifle to hold a license, issued only after a fingerprint-based nationwide background check, with a photo ID card renewed every five years and a fee capped at $10.

Requires all sales and transfers of qualifying guns to be processed by a licensed dealer, who reports the make, model, and serial number to a new federal record-of-sale system within 14 days, so police can trace crime guns.

Makes it a crime to fail to report a lost or stolen qualifying gun within 72 hours and to keep a loaded gun accessible to a child who then kills or injures someone, with exceptions for secured storage and lawful self-defense.

Requires private transfers to go through a dealer, closing the gap that lets sales between strangers happen with no background check, while exempting gifts within families and loans for hunting or at a range.

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of gun owners, who would need a federal license, fingerprints, and a dealer-processed transfer for every sale of a covered gun, facing up to 10 years in prison for unlicensed possession; firearms dealers and manufacturers, who bear new recordkeeping, reporting, and inspection duties. [S2]

drawbacks.text: Possessing a covered gun without a license would carry up to 10 years in prison, so otherwise law-abiding owners who missed a renewal or paperwork deadline would face felony exposure.

The bill repeals the existing federal statute that prohibits establishing a registration system and directs dealers to file sale reports with the Attorney General, which critics read as creating a federal list of gun owners even though the text disclaims a national registry.

Applicants must certify they were not a patient in a mental health facility in the past five years and authorize release of mental health records, a broad disqualifier that mental health advocates have long warned discourages people from seeking care.
Rural owners far from a licensed dealer would have to travel and pay dealer transfer fees for every private sale or family handoff outside the narrow exemptions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Licensing and record-of-sale systems in states that use them are associated with fewer gun deaths and better tracing, and the fee cap and family-transfer exemptions soften the burden. But the bill's reach is sweeping: it converts what is today an unlicensed right for tens of millions of owners into a federal permit system with felony penalties, a national sale ledger, and new mental-health disqualifiers. The design tradeoff is real, and the bill never received a hearing where it could have been tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2024 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Duckworth introduced the Blair Holt Firearm Owner Licensing and Record of Sale Act on May 9, 2024, named for a Chicago student killed shielding a classmate on a school bus in 2007.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was its last action of any kind.
No senator joined as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill would have required a federal license to possess a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine, routed all transfers through licensed dealers, and repealed the existing federal prohibition on establishing a firearms registration system.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and the firearms industry are better off, because the licensing, dealer-transfer, and record-of-sale requirements never took effect; no one gained any new protections, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it for Blair Holt, a Chicago student killed on a school bus in 2007; it was her bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee on May 9, 2024; the bill shows no committee action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Gun rights advocacy groups, including the NRA
against.what_they_did: Have long campaigned against federal gun licensing and registration proposals of this kind, and such bills carry no cosponsor support in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only signal is that a Democratic senator's gun-licensing bill drew zero cosponsors from either party in a Senate with 48 Democrats, 4 independents, and 49 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have made dealers the checkpoint for every private transfer, required 14-day sale reports, allowed Justice Department inspections, and subjected manufacturers to sales reporting. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the public-safety purpose its supporters claimed, since its revenue depends on unrestricted sales.

Tens of millions of owners of handguns and modern sporting rifles would have faced a federal license, fingerprinting, dealer-mediated transfers, and up to 10 years in prison for violations. Some gun owners also benefit from policies that keep guns away from prohibited buyers, but the bill's costs would fall on them directly.
